Global weak solutions to a fractional
Cahn–Hilliard cross-diffusion system
in lymphangiogenesisThanks: The authors acknowledge partial support from the Austrian Science Fund (FWF), grants P33010 and F65. This work has received funding from the European Research Council (ERC) under the European Union’s Horizon 2020 research and innovation programme, ERC Advanced Grant no. 101018153.

Ansgar Jüngel Address: Institute of Analysis and Scientific Computing, Technische Universität, Wiedner Hauptstraße 8–10, 1040 Wien, Austria Email address: juengel@tuwien.ac.at and Yue Li Address: Institute of Analysis and Scientific Computing, Technische Universität, Wiedner Hauptstraße 8-10, 1040 Wien, Austria Email address: yue.li@asc.tuwien.ac.at
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

A spectral-fractional Cahn–Hilliard cross-diffusion system, which describes the pre-patterning of lymphatic vessel morphology in collagen gels, is studied. The model consists of two higher-order quasilinear parabolic equations and describes the evolution of the fiber phase volume fraction and the solute concentration. The free energy consists of the nonconvex Flory–Huggins energy and a fractional gradient energy, modeling nonlocal long-range correlations. The existence of global weak solutions to this system in a bounded domain with no-flux boundary conditions is shown. The proof is based on a three-level approximation scheme, spectral-fractional calculus, and a priori estimates coming from the energy inequality.

Key words and phrases: 
Cahn–Hilliard equation; cross-diffusion equations; spectral-fractional Laplacian; singular potential; free energy; weak solutions.
2000 Mathematics Subject Classification
35D30, 35K35, 35K65, 35K67, 92C37.

1. Introduction

The pre-patterning of lymphatic vessel morphology in collagen gels was modeled by Roose and Fowler [25] using evolution equations for the fiber phase volume fraction ϕ⁡(x,t)\phi(x,t) and the concentration c⁡(x,t)c(x,t) of the solute. The model consists of a cross-diffusion system of Cahn–Hilliard type solved in a bounded domain with no-flux boundary conditions. It was shown in [22] that a modified form of this model is thermodynamically consistent in the sense that the evolution is a gradient flow associated to the free energy

Eloc​(ϕ,c)=∫ℝd(12​|∇ϕ|2+f⁡(ϕ,c))​𝑑x,\displaystyle E_{\rm loc}(\phi,c)=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}\bigg(\frac{1}{2}|\nabla\phi|^{2}+f(\phi,c)\bigg)dx,

which is the sum of the correlation energy density 12​|∇ϕ|2\frac{1}{2}|\nabla\phi|^{2} and the interaction-nutrient energy density f⁡(ϕ,c)f(\phi,c). The equations model the separation of the phases ϕ=0\phi=0 and ϕ=1\phi=1 described by local short-range interactions. Nonlocal long-range interactions may occur as well [28], leading to nonlocal free energies of the type

Enonloc​(ϕ,c)=∫ℝd(14​∫ℝd∫ℝdJ⁡(x−y)​(ϕ⁡(x)−ϕ⁡(y))2​𝑑x​𝑑y+f⁡(ϕ,c))​𝑑x,\displaystyle E_{\rm nonloc}(\phi,c)=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}\bigg(\frac{1}{4}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}J(x-y)(\phi(x)-\phi(y))^{2}dxdy+f(\phi,c)\bigg)dx,

where JJ is an integral kernel. We refer to [7, 19] for physical justifications of this approach. We wish to consider nonsmooth kernels close to the Laplacian and choose a fractional Laplacian operator. While there is a natural definition of the fractional Laplacian in the whole space, its definition in bounded domains may differ. In this paper, we use the spectral-fractional Laplacian definition. An existence analysis of the gradient-flow equations associated to the energy ElocE_{\rm loc} was given in [21]. Our aim is to extend this analysis for the gradient-flow equations associated to a free energy in which the gradient term in ElocE_{\rm loc} is replaced by a fractional gradient term.

1.1. Model equations

More precisely, the diffusion system for lymphangiogenesis reads as

(1.1) ∂tϕ\displaystyle\partial_{t}\phi =div(M(ϕ)(∇μ−c∇∂cf(ϕ,c))),\displaystyle=\operatorname{div}\big(M(\phi)(\nabla\mu-c\nabla\partial_{c}f(\phi,c))\big),
(1.2) ∂tc\displaystyle\partial_{t}c =−div(cM(ϕ)(∇μ−c∇∂cf(ϕ,c)))+div(ce−ϕ∇∂cf(ϕ,c)),\displaystyle=-\operatorname{div}\big(cM(\phi)(\nabla\mu-c\nabla\partial_{c}f(\phi,c))\big)+\operatorname{div}\big(ce^{-\phi}\nabla\partial_{c}f(\phi,c)\big),
(1.3) μ\displaystyle\mu =(−Δ)Ωsϕ+∂ϕf(ϕ,c)in Ω,t>0,\displaystyle=(-\Delta)^{s}_{\Omega}\phi+\partial_{\phi}f(\phi,c)\quad\mbox{in }\Omega,\ t>0,

where Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{d} (d≥1d\geq 1) is a bounded domain, ∂c=∂/∂c\partial_{c}=\partial/\partial c, ∂ϕ=∂/∂ϕ\partial_{\phi}=\partial/\partial\phi are partial derivatives, and (−Δ)Ωs(-\Delta)^{s}_{\Omega} is the spectral-fractional Laplacian on its domain D⁡((−Δ)Ωs)⊂L2​(Ω)D((-\Delta)^{s}_{\Omega})\subset L^{2}(\Omega) with parameter 0<s<10<s<1, defined by the spectral decomposition

(−Δ)Ωs​ϕ=∑k=1∞λks​(ϕ,ek)L2​(Ω)​ek,ϕ∈D⁡((−Δ)Ωs),\displaystyle(-\Delta)_{\Omega}^{s}\phi=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\lambda_{k}^{s}(\phi,e_{k})_{L^{2}(\Omega)}e_{k},\quad\phi\in D((-\Delta)^{s}_{\Omega}),

where (ek,λk)(e_{k},\lambda_{k}) are the eigenpairs of the Laplacian −Δ-\Delta with homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions; see Section 2 for details. One may use the Riesz fractional Laplacian as well, but the spectral-fractional Laplacian requires no information about ϕ\phi in the exterior ℝd∖Ω{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\setminus\Omega [24].

The mobility M⁡(ϕ)M(\phi) is assumed to be nondegenerate, i.e., it is strictly positive, and the Flory–Huggins energy density is given by

(1.4) f⁡(ϕ,c)=ϕ​log⁡ϕ+(1−ϕ)​log⁡(1−ϕ)+ϕ⁡(1−ϕ)+c22+c⁡(1−ϕ)+log⁡2.f(\phi,c)=\phi\log\phi+(1-\phi)\log(1-\phi)+\phi(1-\phi)+\frac{c^{2}}{2}+c(1-\phi)+\log 2.

The first three terms describe the (nonconvex) Flory–Huggins energy [15, 20], while the last three terms represent the nutrient energy [18, (2.63)]. Equations (1.1)–(1.3) are supplemented by initial and no-flux boundary conditions,

(1.5) ϕ⁡(0)=ϕ0,c⁡(0)=c0\displaystyle\phi(0)=\phi_{0},\quad c(0)=c_{0} in ​Ω,\displaystyle\quad\mbox{in }\Omega,
(1.6) ∇ϕ⋅ν=c∇c⋅ν=∇μ⋅ν=0\displaystyle\nabla\phi\cdot\nu=c\nabla c\cdot\nu=\nabla\mu\cdot\nu=0 on ​∂Ω,t>0.\displaystyle\quad\mbox{on }\partial\Omega,\ t>0.

The goal of this paper is to prove the existence of global weak solutions.

1.2. Key ideas

The free energy of system (1.1)–(1.3) reads as

E⁡(ϕ,c)=∫Ω(12​|(−Δ)Ωs/2​ϕ|2+f⁡(ϕ,c))​𝑑x.\displaystyle E(\phi,c)=\int_{\Omega}\bigg(\frac{1}{2}|(-\Delta)_{\Omega}^{s/2}\phi|^{2}+f(\phi,c)\bigg)dx.

Thanks to the thermodynamically consistent modeling, the free energy is a Lyapunov functional and the following energy equality is satisfied:

(1.7) d​Ed​t(ϕ,c)+∫ΩM(ϕ)|∇μ−c∇∂cf(ϕ,c)|2dx+∫Ωce−ϕ|∇∂cf(ϕ,c)|2dx=0.\displaystyle\frac{dE}{dt}(\phi,c)+\int_{\Omega}M(\phi)|\nabla\mu-c\nabla\partial_{c}f(\phi,c)|^{2}dx+\int_{\Omega}ce^{-\phi}|\nabla\partial_{c}f(\phi,c)|^{2}dx=0.

Interestingly, the energy dissipation is the same as in the local model of [21]. However, since s<1s<1, we obtain less regularity than in [21], which makes the analysis more delicate. Further difficulties are the degeneracy at c=0c=0 and the singularity of the potential ∂ϕf⁡(ϕ,c)\partial_{\phi}f(\phi,c) at ϕ=0\phi=0 and ϕ=1\phi=1. Unlike [21], we assume a nondegenerate mobility, which allows us to overcome the mentioned difficulties.

The main task is the derivation of an a priori bound for μ\mu in some Sobolev space. Clearly, in the degenerate case, a gradient bound cannot be expected. We first estimate as follows:

‖∇μ‖L2​(0,T,L4/3​(Ω))\displaystyle\|\nabla\mu\|_{L^{2}(0,T;L^{4/3}(\Omega))} ≤C∥∇μ−c∇∂cf(ϕ,c)∥L2​(0,T,L4/3​(Ω))\displaystyle\leq C\|\nabla\mu-c\nabla\partial_{c}f(\phi,c)\|_{L^{2}(0,T;L^{4/3}(\Omega))}
+∥c∥L∞​(0,T,L4​(Ω))∥c∇∂cf(ϕ,c)∥L2​(0,T,L2​(Ω)).\displaystyle\phantom{xx}+\|\sqrt{c}\|_{L^{\infty}(0,T;L^{4}(\Omega))}\|\sqrt{c}\nabla\partial_{c}f(\phi,c)\|_{L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(\Omega))}.

The right-hand side is bounded thanks to the energy equality (1.7) (here we use the positivity of M⁡(ϕ)M(\phi)). To estimate μ\mu in L1​(Ω)L^{1}(\Omega), we use equation (1.3):

∫Ωμ​𝑑x\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\mu dx =∫Ω((−Δ)Ωs​ϕ+∂ϕf⁡(ϕ,c))​𝑑x=∫Ω∂ϕf⁡(ϕ,c)​𝑑x.\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}\big((-\Delta)^{s}_{\Omega}\phi+\partial_{\phi}f(\phi,c)\big)dx=\int_{\Omega}\partial_{\phi}f(\phi,c)dx.

The idea is to estimate the integral over ∂ϕf⁡(ϕ,c)\partial_{\phi}f(\phi,c) in terms of ∇μ\nabla\mu, using (1.3) again and some techniques from [16]. Then

‖∫Ωμ​𝑑x‖L2​(0,T)≤C​‖∇μ‖L2​(0,T,L4/3​(Ω))+C≤C,\displaystyle\bigg\|\int_{\Omega}\mu dx\bigg\|_{L^{2}(0,T)}\leq C\|\nabla\mu\|_{L^{2}(0,T;L^{4/3}(\Omega))}+C\leq C,

where C>0C>0 is a constant independent of the solution. The Poincaré–Wirtinger inequality provides a bound for μ\mu in L2​(0,T,L4/3​(Ω))L^{2}(0,T;L^{4/3}(\Omega)). This is the key estimate for deriving further bounds for (−Δ)Ωs​ϕ(-\Delta)_{\Omega}^{s}\phi in L2​(0,T,L2​(Ω))L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(\Omega)) and for c3/2c^{3/2} in L2​(0,T,W1,4/3​(Ω))L^{2}(0,T;W^{1,4/3}(\Omega)).

Compared to our previous work [21], we are able to derive a gradient bound for μ\mu. This was compensated in [21] by the computation of an entropy inequality yielding an L2​(Ω)L^{2}(\Omega) bound for Δ​ϕ\Delta\phi. Such an estimate cannot be expected in our case, and we obtain only a bound for (−Δ)Ωs​ϕ(-\Delta)_{\Omega}^{s}\phi in L2​(Ω)L^{2}(\Omega) (recall that s<1s<1). However, this estimate is sufficient even without the use of the entropy functional.

To derive a bound for (−Δ)Ωs​ϕ(-\Delta)_{\Omega}^{s}\phi, we split the Flory–Huggins potential in the singular part f1′​(ϕ)=log⁡ϕ−log⁡(1−ϕ)f_{1}^{\prime}(\phi)=\log\phi-\log(1-\phi) and the regular part ∂ϕf2​(ϕ,c)=1−2​ϕ−c\partial_{\phi}f_{2}(\phi,c)=1-2\phi-c and multiply (1.3) by (−Δ)Ωs​ϕ(-\Delta)_{\Omega}^{s}\phi:

(1.8) ∫Ω|\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}| (−Δ)Ωsϕ|2dx+∫Ωf1′(ϕ)(−Δ)Ωsϕdx\displaystyle(-\Delta)_{\Omega}^{s}\phi|^{2}dx+\int_{\Omega}f^{\prime}_{1}(\phi)(-\Delta)_{\Omega}^{s}\phi dx
=∫Ωμ​(−Δ)Ωs​ϕ​𝑑x+∫Ω(c−1+2​ϕ)​(−Δ)Ωs​ϕ​𝑑x\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}\mu(-\Delta)_{\Omega}^{s}\phi dx+\int_{\Omega}(c-1+2\phi)(-\Delta)_{\Omega}^{s}\phi dx
≤12​‖(−Δ)Ωs​ϕ‖L2​(Ω)2+‖μ‖L2​(Ω)2+‖c−1+2​ϕ‖L2​(Ω)2.\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\|(-\Delta)_{\Omega}^{s}\phi\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}^{2}+\|\mu\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}^{2}+\|c-1+2\phi\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}^{2}.

The first term on the right-hand side can be absorbed by the left-hand side. Since we already proved that μ\mu is bounded in W1,4/3​(Ω)↪L2​(Ω)W^{1,4/3}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^{2}(\Omega) (the embedding holds in up to four dimensions), the last two terms on the right-hand side are bounded. It was shown in [27, Theorem 3.3] that the second term on the left-hand side of (1.8) is nonnegative, which can be interpreted as a weak form of the Stroock–Varapoulos inequality. However, this result only holds true if f1′′f_{1}^{\prime\prime} is uniformly bounded, which is not true in our case. Therefore, we need to approximate f1′f_{1}^{\prime} by some function f1,δ′f^{\prime}_{1,\delta} with some parameter δ>0\delta>0. With these arguments, we see that (−Δ)Ωs​ϕ(-\Delta)_{\Omega}^{s}\phi is bounded in L2​(Ω)L^{2}(\Omega) for an approximation of ϕ\phi. These are the key estimates for the existence analysis. The limit δ→0\delta\to 0 can be performed by using the a priori estimates and compactness arguments.

1.3. Main result

We first detail our definition of weak solution. Set ΩT=Ω×(0,T)\Omega_{T}=\Omega\times(0,T) and ϕ¯0=meas​(Ω)−1​∫Ωϕ0​𝑑x\overline{\phi}_{0}=\mbox{meas}(\Omega)^{-1}\int_{\Omega}\phi_{0}dx.

Definition 1.1 (Weak solution).

Let T>0T>0 be arbitrary and let 1/2≤s<11/2\leq s<1. The function (ϕ,c)(\phi,c) is called a weak solution to problem (1.1)–(1.6) on [0,T][0,T] if (ϕ,c)(\phi,c) satisfies 0<ϕ<10<\phi<1, c≥0c\geq 0 in ΩT\Omega_{T},

ϕ∈L∞​(0,T,D⁡((−Δ)Ωs/2))∩L2​(0,T,D⁡((−Δ)Ωs)),μ∈L2​(0,T,W1,4/3​(Ω)),\displaystyle\phi\in L^{\infty}(0,T;D((-\Delta)^{s/2}_{\Omega}))\cap L^{2}(0,T;D((-\Delta)^{s}_{\Omega})),\quad\mu\in L^{2}(0,T;W^{1,4/3}(\Omega)),
c∈L∞​(0,T,L2​(Ω)),c3/2∈L4/3​(0,T,W1,4/3​(Ω)),\displaystyle c\in L^{\infty}(0,T;L^{2}(\Omega)),\quad c^{3/2}\in L^{4/3}(0,T;W^{1,4/3}(\Omega)),
M(ϕ)(∇μ−c∇∂cf(ϕ,c))∈L2(ΩT),c∇∂cf(ϕ,c)∈L2(ΩT),\displaystyle M(\phi)(\nabla\mu-c\nabla\partial_{c}f(\phi,c))\in L^{2}(\Omega_{T}),\quad\sqrt{c}\nabla\partial_{c}f(\phi,c)\in L^{2}(\Omega_{T}),
∂tϕ∈L2​(0,T,H1​(Ω)′),∂tc∈L3/2​(0,T,W1,9​(Ω)′),\displaystyle\partial_{t}\phi\in L^{2}(0,T;H^{1}(\Omega)^{\prime}),\quad\partial_{t}c\in L^{3/2}(0,T;W^{1,9}(\Omega)^{\prime}),

the initial conditions ϕ⁡(0)=ϕ0\phi(0)=\phi_{0} in L2​(Ω)L^{2}(\Omega), c⁡(0)=c0c(0)=c_{0} in the sense of H1​(Ω)′H^{1}(\Omega)^{\prime}, (ϕ,c)(\phi,c) verifies the weak formulation

∫0T⟨∂tϕ,ψ1⟩1​𝑑t\displaystyle\int_{0}^{T}\langle\partial_{t}\phi,\psi_{1}\rangle_{1}dt =−∫0T∫ΩM(ϕ)(∇μ−c∇∂cf(ϕ,c))⋅∇ψ1dxdt,\displaystyle=-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}M(\phi)(\nabla\mu-c\nabla\partial_{c}f(\phi,c))\cdot\nabla\psi_{1}dxdt,
∫0T⟨∂tc,ψ2⟩2​𝑑t\displaystyle\int_{0}^{T}\langle\partial_{t}c,\psi_{2}\rangle_{2}dt =∫0T∫ΩcM(ϕ)(∇μ−c∇∂cf(ϕ,c))⋅∇ψ2dxdt\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}cM(\phi)(\nabla\mu-c\nabla\partial_{c}f(\phi,c))\cdot\nabla\psi_{2}dxdt
−∫0T∫Ωce−ϕ∇∂cf(ϕ,c)⋅∇ψ2dxdt\displaystyle\phantom{xx}-\int^{T}_{0}\int_{\Omega}ce^{-\phi}\nabla\partial_{c}f(\phi,c)\cdot\nabla\psi_{2}dxdt

for all ψ1∈L2​(0,T,H1​(Ω))\psi_{1}\in L^{2}(0,T;H^{1}(\Omega)), ψ2∈L3​(0,T,W1,9​(Ω))\psi_{2}\in L^{3}(0,T;W^{1,9}(\Omega)), and μ\mu satisfies

μ=(−Δ)Ωs​ϕ+∂ϕf⁡(ϕ,c)a.e. in ​ΩT.\mu=(-\Delta)_{\Omega}^{s}\phi+\partial_{\phi}f(\phi,c)\quad\mbox{a.e.\ in }\Omega_{T}.

Here, ⟨⋅,⋅⟩1\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{1} is the dual product between H1​(Ω)′H^{1}(\Omega)^{\prime} and H1​(Ω)H^{1}(\Omega), and ⟨⋅,⋅⟩2\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{2} is the dual product between W1,9​(Ω)′W^{1,9}(\Omega)^{\prime} and W1,9​(Ω)W^{1,9}(\Omega).

Now we state our main result.

Theorem 1.2.

Assume that Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{d} (d≤3)(d\leq 3) is a bounded domain with smooth boundary and let 1/2≤s<11/2\leq s<1, T>0T>0. The mobility MM is continuous on ℝ{\mathbb{R}} and satisfies

γ≤M⁡(s)≤1/γfor any ​s∈ℝ\displaystyle\gamma\leq M(s)\leq 1/\gamma\quad\mbox{for any }s\in{\mathbb{R}}

for positive constant γ\gamma. Let ϕ0∈D⁡((−Δ)Ωs/2)\phi_{0}\in D((-\Delta)^{s/2}_{\Omega}), c0∈L2​(Ω)c_{0}\in L^{2}(\Omega) satisfy 0<ϕ¯0<10<\overline{\phi}_{0}<1, 0≤ϕ0≤10\leq\phi_{0}\leq 1 and c0≥0c_{0}\geq 0 in Ω\Omega. Then problem (1.1)–(1.6) possesses a weak solution (ϕ,c)(\phi,c) in [0,T][0,T] in the sense of Definition 1.1.

Since we need to define ∇ϕ\nabla\phi in L2​(Ω)L^{2}(\Omega) in the weak formulation, the embedding ϕ∈D⁡((−Δ)Ωs)↪H1​(Ω)\phi\in D((-\Delta)_{\Omega}^{s})\hookrightarrow H^{1}(\Omega) is required, explaining the lower bound s≥1/2s\geq 1/2. The restriction of the space dimension basically comes from the embedding W1,4/3​(Ω)↪L2​(Ω)W^{1,4/3}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^{2}(\Omega) which holds up to d≤4d\leq 4. We believe that our results hold true if d=4d=4 at the expense of the integrability of the unknowns. The condition 0<ϕ¯0<10<\overline{\phi}_{0}<1 is used in Lemma 5.1 to estimate an approximation of f1′​(ϕ)f^{\prime}_{1}(\phi) in L1​(Ω)L^{1}(\Omega). Note that the initial phases may vanish in certain regions, but their integrals need to be positive.

Concerning the proof of Theorem 1.2, the complicated structure of system (1.1)–(1.3) makes a three-level approximation necessary. First, we remove the singularity in f′​(ϕ,c)f^{\prime}(\phi,c) by truncation using the parameter δ>0\delta>0. Furthermore, we add some articial diffusion of order δ\delta to the equations for cc and μ\mu, and we mollify the initial data. Second, we truncate the diffusion coefficient cc in the equation (1.2) for the solute concentration by using a parameter ε>0\varepsilon>0. Third, we solve the approximate problem by the Faedo–Galerkin method involving the dimension N∈ℕN\in{\mathbb{N}} of the Faedo–Galerkin space.

The Faedo–Galerkin system is solved by applying Peano’s theorem. Thanks to the approximate energy equality and the artificial diffusion, we can pass to the limits N→∞N\to\infty and ε→0\varepsilon\to 0. The delicate part of the proof is the limit δ→0\delta\to 0. For this, we derive additional estimates as described in Section 1.2 and apply a nonlinear version of the Aubin–Lions compactness lemma in the version of [8] to obtain the existence of a subsequence of an approximating sequence that converges to a weak solution (ϕ,c,μ)(\phi,c,\mu) to (1.1)–(1.6).

1.4. State of the art

Before we prove Theorem 1.2, we briefly comment on the state of the art. While multi-phase models are intensively studied in the literature in the context of, for instance, tumor [11] and biofilm growth [29] since several years, the two-phase modeling of lymphoangiogenesis is more recent [25]. It was found in [26] that a hexagonal lymphatic capillary network is optimal in terms of fluid drainage, confirmed by experiments in mouse tails and human skin. A hexagonal pre-structure was found in numerical simulations in two space dimensions [22].

The Cahn–Hilliard equation ∂tϕ−Δ⁡(−Δ​ϕ+f′​(ϕ))=0\partial_{t}\phi-\Delta(-\Delta\phi+f^{\prime}(\phi))=0 with the (possibly singular) potential f′​(ϕ)f^{\prime}(\phi) was introduced in [6] to study phase separation in binary alloys. The local and nonlocal equations were derived in [19] from a lattice gas evolving via Kawasaki exchange with respect to the Gibbs measure for a Hamiltonian. The localization limit was proved both in the nondegenerate [10] and degenerate case [12].

The existence of one-dimensional solutions to the (local) Cahn–Hilliard equation was first proved in [14] and later extended to several space dimensions in [13]. The existence and uniqueness of solutions to the Cahn–Hilliard system strictly depend on the properties of the mobility M⁡(ϕ)M(\phi) (being degenerate or nondegenerate) and the potential f′​(ϕ)f^{\prime}(\phi) (being singular or regular). A mathematical difficulty is the fourth-order derivative, which excludes the use of comparison principles. A sufficient condition for the property 0≤ϕ≤10\leq\phi\leq 1 (if satisfied initially) is a degenerate mobility M⁡(ϕ)M(\phi) [30] or a singular potential [5].

The study of fractional Cahn–Hilliard equations has recently received considerable attention. In [1], the fractional version

∂tϕ+(−Δ)Ωs​(−Δ​ϕ+f′​(ϕ))=0\displaystyle\partial_{t}\phi+(-\Delta)_{\Omega}^{s}(-\Delta\phi+f^{\prime}(\phi))=0

was identified as a gradient flow of the free energy ElocE_{\rm loc} in the negative-order fractional Sobolev space H−s​(Ω)H^{-s}(\Omega) with 0<s<10<s<1, and the existence of weak solutions was proved. On the other hand, the H−1​(Ω)H^{-1}(\Omega) gradient flow of the fractional free energy becomes

∂tϕ−Δ⁡((−Δ)Ωs​ϕ+f′​(ϕ))=0,\displaystyle\partial_{t}\phi-\Delta\big((-\Delta)_{\Omega}^{s}\phi+f^{\prime}(\phi)\big)=0,

which was investigated in a bounded domain with periodic boundary conditions [2] and with no-flux boundary conditions [17]. Finally, the double-fractional Cahn–Hilliard equation

∂tϕ+(−Δ)Ωs​((−Δ)Ωσ​ϕ+f′​(ϕ))=0,\displaystyle\partial_{t}\phi+(-\Delta)_{\Omega}^{s}\big((-\Delta)_{\Omega}^{\sigma}\phi+f^{\prime}(\phi)\big)=0,

with 0<s,σ<10<s,\sigma<1 and the singular integral representation of the fractional Laplacian was analyzed in [3, 4]. Instead of the fractional Laplacian, fractional powers of self-adjoint monotone operators were considered in [9]. We are not aware of papers on systems of fractional Cahn–Hilliard equations. Thus, up to our knowledge, the existence analysis of the spectral-fractional Cahn–Hilliard cross-diffusion system (1.1)–(1.3) is new.

The paper is organized as follows. We recall the definition and some properties of the spectral-fractional Laplacian in Section 2. The approximate solution in the Faedo–Galerkin space and the limit N→∞N\to\infty are proved in Section 3. The limit ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 is performed in Section 4, while the more involved limit δ→0\delta\to 0 is shown in Section 5.

2. The spectral-fractional Laplacian

We introduce the spectral-fractional Laplacian and recall some of its properties. We refer to [17, Sec. 2.1] for details. The operator (−Δ)Ω(-\Delta)_{\Omega} denotes the Laplace operator −Δ-\Delta with homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions with domain

D((−Δ)Ω):={u∈H2(Ω):∇u⋅ν=0 on ∂Ω}.\displaystyle D((-\Delta)_{\Omega}):=\{u\in H^{2}(\Omega):\nabla u\cdot\nu=0\mbox{ on }\partial\Omega\}.

By spectral theory, there exists a sequence of real nonnegative eigenvalues (λk)k∈ℕ(\lambda_{k})_{k\in{\mathbb{N}}} satisfying λ0=0\lambda_{0}=0, λk≤λk+1\lambda_{k}\leq\lambda_{k+1} for k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}}, and λk→∞\lambda_{k}\to\infty as k→∞k\to\infty. The sequence of associated eigenfunctions (ek)k∈ℕ⊂D⁡((−Δ)Ω)(e_{k})_{k\in{\mathbb{N}}}\subset D((-\Delta)_{\Omega}) form an orthonormal basis of L2​(Ω)L^{2}(\Omega). The eigenfunctions verify (−Δ)Ω​ek=λk​ek(-\Delta)_{\Omega}e_{k}=\lambda_{k}e_{k} in Ω\Omega and e¯k:=|Ω|−1​∫Ωek​𝑑x=0\overline{e}_{k}:=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_{\Omega}e_{k}dx=0 for k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}}. We construct a regularized problem associated to (1.1)–(1.6) by approximating the singular part of the energy density and truncating the concentration-dependent diffusion coefficients. To this end, we split the free energy density (1.4) into a convex part f1f_{1} and a nonconvex part f2f_{2},

As in [16, (3.5)] (but different from [21]), we define an approximation f1,δf_{1,\delta} of f1f_{1} on ℝ{\mathbb{R}} to remove the singularities at ϕ=0\phi=0 and ϕ=1\phi=1. There exists a convex function f1,δ:ℝ→ℝf_{1,\delta}:{\mathbb{R}}\to{\mathbb{R}} such that f1,δ′f_{1,\delta}^{\prime} is Lipschitz continuous on ℝ{\mathbb{R}} with constant 1/δ1/\delta and f1,δ​(1/2)=f1,δ′​(1/2)=0f_{1,\delta}(1/2)=f_{1,\delta}^{\prime}(1/2)=0. +δ​‖∇cδ‖L2​(ΩT)​‖∇ψ‖L2​(ΩT)≤C​‖ψ‖L3​(0,T,W1,9​(Ω)).\displaystyle+\delta\|\nabla c_{\delta}\|_{L^{2}(\Omega_{T})}\|\nabla\psi\|_{L^{2}(\Omega_{T})}\leq C\|\psi\|_{L^{3}(0,T;W^{1,9}(\Omega))}.

This finishes the proof the first claim of (5.12). Similarly, we obtain the second claim of (5.12). ∎

5.2. Limit δ→0\delta\to 0

In this section, we perform the limit δ→0\delta\to 0 in the weak formulation of (4.6)–(4.8). We deduce from bounds (5.1), (5.5), and (5.9) that there exist subsequences (not relabeled) such that, as δ→0\delta\to 0,

ϕδ⇀∗ϕ\displaystyle\phi_{\delta}\rightharpoonup^{*}\phi weakly* in ​L∞​(0,T,Ds​(Ω))∩L2​(0,T,D2​s​(Ω)),\displaystyle\quad\mbox{weakly* in }L^{\infty}(0,T;D^{s}(\Omega))\cap L^{2}(0,T;D^{2s}(\Omega)),
∇ϕδ⇀∇ϕ\displaystyle\nabla\phi_{\delta}\rightharpoonup\nabla\phi weakly in ​L2​(ΩT),\displaystyle\quad\mbox{weakly in }L^{2}(\Omega_{T}),
μδ⇀μ\displaystyle\mu_{\delta}\rightharpoonup\mu weakly in ​L2​(ΩT)∩L2​(0,T,W1,4/3​(Ω)).\displaystyle\quad\mbox{weakly in }L^{2}(\Omega_{T})\cap L^{2}(0,T;W^{1,4/3}(\Omega)).

In view of the compact embedding Ds​(Ω)↪L2​(Ω)D^{s}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^{2}(\Omega) for s>0s>0, the bounds (5.1) and (5.12) for ϕδ\phi_{\delta} allow us to apply the Aubin–Lions lemma to infer that, up to a subsequence,

ϕδ→ϕstrongly in ​C​([0,T],L2​(Ω)).\displaystyle\phi_{\delta}\rightarrow\phi\quad\mbox{strongly in }C([0,T];L^{2}(\Omega)).

This implies that

M⁡(ϕδ)→M⁡(ϕ),e−[ϕδ]+1→e−[ϕ]+1strongly in ​Lp​(ΩT)​ for ​p∈[1,∞).\displaystyle M(\phi_{\delta})\rightarrow M(\phi),\quad e^{-[\phi_{\delta}]^{1}_{+}}\rightarrow e^{-[\phi]^{1}_{+}}\quad\mbox{strongly in }L^{p}(\Omega_{T})\mbox{ for }p\in[1,\infty).

Next, we prove that 0<ϕ<10<\phi<1 a.e. in ΩT\Omega_{T}. In [21, Lemma 5.3], this follows from the degeneracy of M⁡(ϕ)M(\phi). Since the mobility is not degenerate in our case, we exploit the singularity as in [16, p. 5273]. For the convenience of the reader, we present the full proof.

Lemma 5.5 (Upper and lower bounds for ϕ\phi).

The limit function ϕ\phi satisfies 0<ϕ<10<\phi<1 a.e. in ΩT\Omega_{T}.

Proof.

Let η\eta be a positive constant such that 1/2∈(η,1−η)1/2\in(\eta,1-\eta). Define the sets

Eδη\displaystyle E_{\delta}^{\eta} :={(x,t)∈ΩT:ϕδ​(x,t)>1−η​ or ​ϕδ​(x,t)<η},\displaystyle:=\{(x,t)\in\Omega_{T}:\phi_{\delta}(x,t)>1-\eta\mbox{ or }\phi_{\delta}(x,t)<\eta\},
Eη\displaystyle E^{\eta} :={(x,t)∈ΩT:ϕ⁡(x,t)>1−η​ or ​ϕ​(x,t)<η}.\displaystyle:=\{(x,t)\in\Omega_{T}:\phi(x,t)>1-\eta\mbox{ or }\phi(x,t)<\eta\}.

It follows from ϕδ→ϕ\phi_{\delta}\rightarrow\phi a.e. in ΩT\Omega_{T} and Fatou’s lemma that

(5.13) meas​(Eη)≤lim infδ→0+meas​(Eδη).\displaystyle\mbox{meas}(E^{\eta})\leq\liminf_{\delta\to 0^{+}}\mbox{meas}(E_{\delta}^{\eta}).

Recall that estimate (5.11) gives a uniform bound for f1,δ′​(ϕδ)f^{\prime}_{1,\delta}(\phi_{\delta}) in L1​(ΩT)L^{1}(\Omega_{T}). Since f1,δ′​(x)≤0f^{\prime}_{1,\delta}(x)\leq 0 for x∈(0,1/2]x\in(0,1/2], f1,δ′​(x)≥0f^{\prime}_{1,\delta}(x)\geq 0 for x∈[1/2,1)x\in[1/2,1), and f1,δ′f^{\prime}_{1,\delta} is nondecreasing, we have

C≥‖f1,δ′​(ϕδ)‖L1​(ΩT)≥∫Eδη|f1,δ′​(ϕδ)|​𝑑x​𝑑t≥min⁡{f1,δ′​(1−η),−f1,δ′​(η)}​meas​(Eδη),\displaystyle C\geq\|f^{\prime}_{1,\delta}(\phi_{\delta})\|_{L^{1}(\Omega_{T})}\geq\int_{E_{\delta}^{\eta}}|f^{\prime}_{1,\delta}(\phi_{\delta})|dxdt\geq\min\{f^{\prime}_{1,\delta}(1-\eta),-f^{\prime}_{1,\delta}(\eta)\}\mbox{meas}(E_{\delta}^{\eta}),

which implies that

meas​(Eδη)≤Cmin⁡{f1,δ′​(1−η),−f1,δ′​(η)}.\displaystyle\mbox{meas}(E_{\delta}^{\eta})\leq\frac{C}{\min\{f^{\prime}_{1,\delta}(1-\eta),-f^{\prime}_{1,\delta}(\eta)\}}.

meas​(Eη)\displaystyle\mbox{meas}(E^{\eta}) ≤lim infδ→0meas​(Eδη)≤Cmin⁡{f1′​(1−η),−f1′​(η)}.\displaystyle\leq\liminf_{\delta\rightarrow 0}\mbox{meas}(E_{\delta}^{\eta})\leq\frac{C}{\min\{f^{\prime}_{1}(1-\eta),-f^{\prime}_{1}(\eta)\}}.

meas​{(x,t)∈ΩT:ϕ≥1​ or ​ϕ≤0}=0,\displaystyle\mbox{meas}\{(x,t)\in\Omega_{T}:\phi\geq 1\mbox{ or }\phi\leq 0\}=0,

which completes the proof of the lemma. ∎

The previous lemma shows that f1′​(ϕ)f^{\prime}_{1}(\phi) is well-defined. Then, in view of the a.e. convergence of ϕδ\phi_{\delta}, we have f1,δ′​(ϕδ)→f1′​(ϕ)f^{\prime}_{1,\delta}(\phi_{\delta})\to f^{\prime}_{1}(\phi) a.e. in ΩT\Omega_{T} as δ→0\delta\to 0. The L2​(ΩT)L^{2}(\Omega_{T}) bound of f1,δ′​(ϕδ)f^{\prime}_{1,\delta}(\phi_{\delta}) in (5.11) implies that

cδ→cstrongly in ​L2​(ΩT).\displaystyle c_{\delta}\rightarrow c\quad\mbox{strongly in }L^{2}(\Omega_{T}).
